abstract: The dynamics of necrophagous insect communities and the decomposition of the cadavers they colonise can be modulated by ecological filtering limiting insect access. We examine how different degrees of confinement influence the decomposition of animal carcasses, their colonisation by necrophagous insects, and the link between these two processes. To this end, vertebrate carcasses were placed either outdoors or in sheds with open or closed windows in a replicated experiment. Over two weeks, decomposition and insect abundance were documented daily. The results indicate that increasing confinement altered insect-mediated decomposition processes, delaying the insect-dominated phase while leaving the bacterial-dominated phase unaffected. Thus, in indoor environments, a dissociation of the decomposition sequence normally observed outdoors was observed due to an increasing delay in the colonisation of most insects with increasing confinement. This indicates that buildings can act as ecological filters that structure the accessibility of carcasses to necrophagous insects. In addition, these findings suggest that cadaver decomposition in indoor environments follows a distinct trajectory, with direct consequences for postmortem interval estimations.
